Abstract:
Most robotic hands and grippers rely on actuators with large gearboxes and force sensors for controlling gripping force. However, this might not be ideal for tasks that require the robot to interact with an unstructured and unknown environment. In this paper, we introduce a novel quasi-direct-drive two-fingered robotic hand with variable impedance control in the joint space and Cartesian space. The hand has a total of four degrees of freedom, backdrivable differential gear trains, and four brushless direct current (BLDC) motors. Motor torque is controlled through Field-Oriented Control (FOC) with current sensing. Variable impedance control enables the robotic hand to execute dexterous manipulation tasks safely during environment-robot and human-robot interactions. The quasi-direct-drive actuators eliminate the need for complex tactile/force sensors or precise motion planning when handling environmental contact. A majority-3D-printed assembly makes this a low-cost research platform built with affordable, readily available off-the-shelf components. Experimental validation demonstrates the robotic hand's capability for stable force-closure and form-closure grasps in the presence of disturbances, reliable in-hand manipulation, and safe dynamic manipulations despite contact with the environment.

Abstract:
The employment of robots in numerous emerging applications, e.g., disaster rescue, nuclear waste remediation, and space exploration, is of paramount importance due to their improved safety, flexibility, and productivity. Due to the harsh environmental conditions, the robotic arm joint motors and power electronic drives are vulnerable to electrical faults and mainly contribute to joint failures. To substantially improve the reliability and robustness of the robot arms utilized in remote, hazardous, and safety-critical environments, autonomous fault-tolerant and fail-active operation for these robotic arms experiencing joint failures should be developed. In the literature, many strategies have been proposed for fault prognosis, diagnosis, and health monitoring of electric motors and drives using online data analytics of the fault signature information. Thus, this paper presents an extensive up-to-date review of joint motor types, common fault types, and robot joint fault prognostics, diagnostics, and health management. First, various joint motors are introduced and compared, considering their performance advantages, disadvantages, and wide applications. Furthermore, joint motors for collaborative robotic applications are summarized and compared as illustrative examples. After that, fault types are reviewed with a further classification by fault locations, namely, stator windings, rotors, and bearings. In addition, health monitoring techniques are classified into methods for stator winding, rotor, and bearing faults. These methods are intensively compared with respect to motor and fault types, proposed health monitoring techniques, and control strategies. Finally, conclusions and future research trends are summarized.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Fatigue is one of the main causes for in service failure of mechanical components and structures. With the development of new materials, such as high strength aluminium or titanium alloys with different microstructures from steels, materials no longer have a fatigue limit in the classical sense, where it was accepted that they would have ‘infinite life’ from 10 million (107) cycles. The emergence of new materials used in critical mechanical parts, including parts obtained from metal additive manufacturing (AM), the need for weight reduction and the ambition to travel greater distances in shorter periods of time, have brought many challenges to design engineers, since they demand predictability of material properties and that they are readily available. Most fatigue testing today still uses uniaxial loads. However, it is generally recognised that multiaxial stresses occur in many full-scale structures, being rare the occurrence of pure uniaxial stress states. By combining both Ultrasonic Fatigue Testing with multiaxial testing through Single-Input-Multiple-Output Modal Analysis, the high costs of both equipment and time to conduct experiments have seen a massive improvement. It is presently possible to test materials under multiaxial loading conditions and for a very high number of cycles in a fraction of the time compared to non-ultrasonic fatigue testing methods (days compared to months or years). This work presents the current status of ultrasonic fatigue testing machines working at a frequency of 20 kHz to date, with emphasis on multiaxial fatigue and very high cycle fatigue. Special attention will be put into the performance of multiaxial fatigue tests of classical cylindrical specimens under tension/torsion and flat cruciform specimens under in-plane bi-axial testing using low cost piezoelectric transducers. Together with the description of the testing machines and associated instrumentation, some experimental results of fatigue tests are presented in order to demonstrate how ultrasonic fatigue testing can be used to determine the behaviour of a steel alloy from a railway wheel at very high cycle fatigue regime when subjected to multiaxial tension/torsion loadings.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Ultrasonic fatigue testing is an increasingly used method to study the high cycle fatigue (HCF) and very high cycle fatigue (VHCF) properties of materials. Specimens are cycled at an ultrasonic frequency, which leads to a drastic reduction of testing times. This work focused on summarising the current understanding, based on literature data and original work, whether and how fatigue properties measured with ultrasonic and conventional equipment are comparable. Aluminium alloys are not strain-rate sensitive. A weaker influence of air humidity at ultrasonic frequencies may lead to prolonged lifetimes in some alloys, and tests in high humidity or distilled water can better approximate environmental conditions at low frequencies. High-strength steels are insensitive to the cycling frequency. Strain rate sensitivity of ferrite causes prolonged lifetimes in those steels that show crack initiation in the ferritic phase. Austenitic stainless steels are less prone to frequency effects. Fatigue properties of titanium alloys and nickel alloys are insensitive to testing frequency. Limited data for magnesium alloys and graphite suggest no frequency influence. Ultrasonic fatigue tests of a glass fibre-reinforced polymer delivered comparable lifetimes to servo-hydraulic tests, suggesting that high-frequency testing is, in principle, applicable to fibre-reinforced polymer composites. The use of equipment with closed-loop control of vibration amplitude and resonance frequency is strongly advised since this guarantees high accuracy and reproducibility of ultrasonic tests. Pulsed loading and appropriate cooling serve to avoid specimen heating.

Abstract:
Pneumatic linear peristaltic actuators can offer some potential advantages when compared with conventional ones. Low cost, virtually unlimited stroke and easy implementation of curved motion profiles are among those benefits. On the downside, these actuators suffer high mechanical stress, which leads to short endurance and increased leakage between chambers during the actuator lifetime. This paper contributes to this field by experimentally characterizing the life behavior of a prototype of a linear pneumatic peristaltic actuator where force—instead of displacement—between rollers is imposed. It is shown that the use of an imposed force configuration has a significant impact in the actuator life time. In fact, the proposed actuator configuration has an average endurance of up to 250% higher than the one previously presented in the literature. This result was obtained while maintaining almost zero leakage between chambers, despite the hose wear throughout the service life. Finally, this paper explores the use of different hose geometries to increase the actuator life span. To this end, a preliminary study is presented where two different 3D printed hose cross sections are tested and compared with a circular one.

Abstract:
With increasing global investment in offshore wind energy and rapid deployment of wind power technologies in deep water hazardous environments, the in-service inspection of wind turbines and their related infrastructure plays an important role in the safe and efficient operation of wind farm fleets. The use of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and remotely piloted aircraft (RPA)—commonly known as “drones”—for remote inspection of wind energy infrastructure has received a great deal of attention in recent years. Drones have significant potential to reduce not only the number of times that personnel will need to travel to and climb up the wind turbines, but also the amount of heavy lifting equipment required to carry out the dangerous inspection works. Drones can also shorten the duration of downtime needed to detect defects and collect diagnostic information from the entire wind farm. Despite all these potential benefits, the drone-based inspection technology in the offshore wind industry is still at an early stage of development and its reliability has yet to be proven. Any unforeseen failure of the drone system during its mission may cause an interruption in inspection operations, and thereby, significant reduction in the electricity generated by wind turbines. In this paper, we propose a semiquantitative reliability analysis framework to identify and evaluate the criticality of mission failures—at both system and component levels—in inspection drones, with the goal of lowering the operation and maintenance (O&M) costs as well as improving personnel safety in offshore wind farms. Our framework is built based upon two well-established failure analysis methodologies, namely, fault tree analysis (FTA) and failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA). It is then tested and verified on a drone prototype, which was developed in the laboratory for taking aerial photography and video of both onshore and offshore wind turbines. The most significant failure modes and underlying root causes within the drone system are identified, and the effects of the failures on the system’s operation are analysed. Finally, some innovative solutions are proposed on how to minimize the risks associated with mission failures in inspection drones.

Abstract:
Operations and maintenance (O&M) of floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) require regular inspection activities to predict, detect, and troubleshoot faults at high altitudes and in harsh environments such as strong winds, waves, and tides. Their costs typically account for more than 30% of the lifetime cost due to high labor costs and long downtime. Different inspection methods, including manual inspection, permanent sensors, climbing robots, remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), can be employed to fulfill O&M missions. The UAVs, as an enabling technology, can deal with time and space constraints easily and complete tasks in a cost-effective and efficient manner, which have been widely used in different industries in recent years. This study provides valuable insights into the existing applications of UAVs in FOWT inspection, highlighting their potential to reduce the inspection cost and thereby reduce the cost of energy production. The article introduces the rationale for applying UAVs to FOWT inspection and examines the current technical status, research gaps, and future directions in this field by conducting a comprehensive literature review over the past 10 years. This paper will also include a review of UAVs’ applications in other infrastructure inspections, such as onshore wind turbines, bridges, power lines, solar power plants, and offshore oil and gas fields, since FOWTs are still in the early stages of development. Finally, the trends of UAV technology and its application in FOWTs inspection are discussed, leading to our future research direction.

The excerpt provides general ISO 9283 repeatability methodology, but it does not report independently measured repeatability or accuracy values for the UR5e, UR5, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova robot arms, and it gives no prices for those robots or their measurement tools. Under the described protocol, testing uses a workspace test cube and a diagonal test plane containing five poses, P1 through P5. The robot is commanded to visit these poses while its actual end-effector pose is measured. Tests use a consistent unidirectional visitation order, 30 cycles per trial, manufacturer-rated velocities of 10%, 50%, and 100%, and rated payload (optionally also 10% payload). Position repeatability is computed from the measured-point cluster: the barycentre is calculated, distances from each measurement to that barycentre are determined, and the specification is the mean distance plus three standard deviations. Orientation repeatability is separately calculated for three rotation angles using three times the standard deviation. The excerpt mentions recording the actual pose and transforming measurements for axial and radial offsets, but it does not identify a specific measurement instrument or provide arm-specific accuracy results.

Reinforcement learning has shown great promise in robotics thanks to its ability to develop efficient robotic control procedures through self-training. In particular, reinforcement learning has been successfully applied to solving the reaching task with robotic arms. In this paper, we define a robust, reproducible and systematic experimental procedure to compare the performance of various model-free algorithms at solving this task. Abstract:
We present CloudGripper, an open source cloud robotics testbed, consisting of a scalable, space and cost- efficient design constructed as a rack of 32 small robot arm work cells. Each robot work cell is fully enclosed and features individual lighting, a low-cost Cartesian robot arm with an attached rotatable parallel jaw gripper and a dual camera setup for experimentation. The system design is focused on continuous operation and features a 10 Gbit/s network connectivity allowing for high throughput remote-controlled experimentation and data collection for robotic manipulation. Furthermore, CloudGripper is intended to form a community testbed to study the challenges of large scale machine learning and cloud and edge-computing in the context of robotic manipulation. In this work, we describe the mechanical design of the system, its initial software stack and evaluate the repeatability of motions executed by the proposed robot arm design. A local network API throughput and latency analysis is also provided. CloudGripper-Rope-100, a dataset of more than a hundred hours of randomized rope pushing interactions and approximately 4 million camera images is collected and serves as a proof of concept demonstrating data collection capabilities. A project website with more information is available at https://cloudgripper.org.

<jats:p>Modern manufacturing robots must dynamically balance multiple conflicting objectives amid rapidly evolving production demands. Traditional control approaches lack the adaptability required for real-time decision-making in Industry 4.0 environments. This study presents an adaptive multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) framework integrating dynamic preference weighting with Pareto-optimal policy discovery for real-time adaptation without manual reconfiguration. Experimental validation employed a UR5 manipulator with RG2 gripper performing quality-aware object sorting in CoppeliaSim with realistic physics (friction μ = 0.4, Bullet engine), manipulating 12 objects across four geometric types on a dynamic conveyor. Thirty independent runs per algorithm (seven baselines, 30,000+ manipulation cycles) demonstrated +24.59% to +34.75% improvements (p < 0.001, d = 0.89–1.52), achieving hypervolume 0.076 ± 0.015 (19.7% coefficient of variation—lowest among all methods) and 95% optimal performance within 180 episodes—five times faster than evolutionary baselines. Four independent verification methods (WFG, PyMOO, Monte Carlo, HSO) confirmed measurement reliability (<0.26% variance). The framework maintains edge computing compatibility (<2 GB RAM, <50 ms latency) and seamless integration with Manufacturing Execution Systems and digital twins. This research establishes new benchmarks for adaptive robotic control in sustainable Industry 4.0/5.0 manufacturing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
We present a novel approach to perform object-independent grasp synthesis from depth images via deep neural networks. Our generative grasping convolutional neural network (GG-CNN) predicts a pixel-wise grasp quality that can be deployed in closed-loop grasping scenarios. GG-CNN overcomes shortcomings in existing techniques, namely discrete sampling of grasp candidates and long computation times. The network is orders of magnitude smaller than other state-of-the-art approaches while achieving better performance, particularly in clutter. Abstract:
Accurate kinematic modelling is pivotal in the safe and reliable execution of both contact and non-contact robotic applications. The kinematic models provided by robot manufacturers are valid only under ideal conditions and it is necessary to account for the manufacturing errors, particularly the joint offsets introduced during the assembling stages, which is identified as the underlying problem for position inaccuracy in more than 90% of the situations. This work was motivated by a very practical need, namely the discrepancy in terms of end-effector kinematics as computed by factory-calibrated internal controller and the nominal kinematic model as per robot datasheet. Even though the problem of robot calibration is not new, the focus is generally on the deployment of external measurement devices (for open loop calibration) or mechanical fixtures (for closed loop calibration). On the other hand, we use the factory-calibrated controller as an ‘oracle’ for our fast-recalibration approach. This allows extracting calibrated intrinsic parameters (e.g., link lengths) otherwise not directly available from the ‘oracle’, for use in ad-hoc control strategies. In this process, we minimize the kinematic mismatch between the ideal and the factory-calibrated robot models for a Kinova Gen3 ultra-lightweight robot by compensating for the joint zero position error and the possible variations in the link lengths. Experimental analysis has been presented to validate the proposed method, followed by the error comparison between the calibrated and un-calibrated models over training and test sets.

Abstract:
—The variety of robotic hand designs and ac- tuation schemes makes it difﬁcult to measure a hand’s graspable volume. For end-users, this lack of standardized measurements makes it challenging to determine a priori if a robot hand is the right size for grasping an object. We propose a practical hand measurement standard, based on precision and power grasps, that is applicable to a wide variety of robot hand designs. The resulting measurements can be used to both determine if an object will ﬁt in the hand and characterize the size of an object with respect to the hand. Our measurement procedure uses a functional approach, based on grasping a hypothetical cylinder, that allows the measurer choose the exact hand orientation and ﬁnger conﬁgurations that are used for the measurements. This ensures that the measurements are functionally comparable while relying on the human to determine the ﬁnger conﬁgurations that best match the intended grasp. We demonstrate using our measurement standard with three commercial robot hand designs and objects from the YCB data set.

Abstract:
Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) have been developed over the years across many nations around the world. IEDs used by terrorist actions and in warfare cause devastating death, injuries and damage. To protect the public, many emergency responders have to risk their lives by performing extremely hazardous tasks such as interacting with suspected IEDs. To prevent the emergency response teams from being negatively impacted by IEDs, many different kinds of response robots have been deployed in many locations worldwide – allowing first responders a safe way to interact with these menaces from a distance. This thesis contributes to the understanding of using robot arms with a Leader–Follower (LF) approach to help humans with performing dexterous operations like those which are inevitably required for manipulating IEDs remotely. The LF approach allows operators to remotely manipulate a robot arm without putting operators’ lives in danger. By physically controlling one arm from a safe distance, operators can successfully copy its movements to a second arm. As a result, we argue, this approach can be helpful for minimizing operator risk when interacting with suspicious devices while at the same time facilitating more intuitive remote control.

The language model matters.


policy reaches 95.1% on LIBERO [16], where clean averages for three protocol-faithful vision-language-
action model (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) evaluations span only 1.36 points [17].  Real2sim
evaluation [18, 19, 20, 21] shows that a carefully built digital twin can predict real-world rankings, but the
prediction is specific to the simulator, policies and setup on which it was validated: in a five-policy study
spanning 1,115 real rollouts across three simulators, SIMPLER showed weak ranking agreement with the
real robot [22]. These studies also mostly run in one direction, placing policies trained on real data inside a
twin. As policies are increasingly trained on simulated data alone [23, 24], a benchmark should also show
that its ranking survives when the same sim-trained weights run on a real robot. Finally, it should measure
what aggregate success hides: a policy can complete a task without understanding it: on LIBERO, a probe that
replaces instruction text with a task-ID embedding nearly matches the best published results [25], and on a real
SO-101, VLAs that manipulate reliably can fail to adapt to OOD spatial relations [10].

We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation with a
single SO-101 arm, built so that its rankings carry over to the real robot (Fig. 1). Its core is an Isaac Lab [26]
digital twin of a real SO-101 setup with 138 household objects in three generalization splits: seen (in the
training dataset), unseen object of a seen class, and unseen class, with 37 unseen-class objects kept private.
Four tasks (place every object in a bin; place an object next to another; place it between two others; move it in
a direction until it reaches the boundary object) are scored automatically from simulator state. They require
the policy to pick out the named object among same-class distractors, grasp unfamiliar geometry and place
it under spatial constraints. The primary evaluation has 916 feasibility-checked episodes over 15 task-family
× split cells, with subsets for held-out appearances (ROBUST), rotating an object to fit a tight space (PLAN)
and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Every learned policy is fine-tuned on the same 3,629 simulated
teleoperated demonstrations of seen objects under an equal 36 h x 4 x A100 compute budget.




                                            2Two studies test whether the twin can stand in for the real robot. Independently trained real-only and sim-only
GR00T N1.6 policies find the same conditions hard (Pearson r = 0.86 across the 15 cells) and fail in the same
ways (Sec. 4). Five policies that never saw real data from our setup, four VLAs and an LLM agent, then run
with identical weights in the twin and on the physical SO-101 in an environment unseen in training, with objects
from all three splits; SO-101 Bench policies work out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen
objects. Simulation ranks them exactly as the real robot does (Spearman ρ = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000, 95% CI
[0.000, 0.169]), although it overestimates every policy’s success by 9 to 31 percentage points (Sec. 5). On the
full leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs, the best learned policies, InternW0-∆[27] and Galaxea 0.5 [28], are
statistically tied near 61; spatial placement and unseen classes are where they fail, and none exceeds 17% on
PLAN. The strongest entry is an LLM agent: GPT-6.1 Sol [29] writing code in the PyRUA-Lean harness [30]
and handing grasps to Galaxea 0.5 scores 83.2 and solves 75% of PLAN. Its lead comes largely from the harness.
On 60 paired episodes, Sol succeeds on 35% (21/60) with direct tool calls, 67% (40/60) with PyRUA-Lean and
85% (51/60) with the Galaxea 0.5 hand-off, against 53% (32/60) for Galaxea 0.5 alone, and the lead holds on
the real robot, 64% (29/45) against 53% (24/45).

Our contributions are:

       • SO-101 Bench, a digital-twin benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on a low-cost
       arm, with instance- and class-level object splits, ROBUST, PLAN and MEM subsets and automatic
        scoring, released with the so101_bench_sim (3,629 simulated episodes) and so101_bench_real
       (∼4,400 real episodes) datasets.

       • Evidence that the twin ranks policies as the real robot does: condition- and failure-level correspon-
       dence between independently trained real-only and sim-only policies, and an exact sim2real ranking of
         five policies, including an LLM agent, run with identical weights and no real data from our setup; these
         policies perform language-conditioned tasks out of the box in an unseen real environment with unseen
         objects.

       • A leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs and two LLM agents, with every learned policy fine-tuned
       on the same data and compute, showing that spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit
        planning remain open.

       • Harness and model ablations showing that, in our setting, a code-as-policy harness that hands grasping
        to a learned policy outperforms either on their own; Direct action generation by the agent proves
        expensive and ineffective, and 6.1 Sol compares favorably to other agents.


2  Related Work

Low-cost hardware and SO-101 benchmarks.  Cheap hardware has repeatedly widened who can do robot
learning. ALOHA showed that a low-cost bimanual rig can learn fine manipulation [31], and 2026 platforms
push prices further, from a $1,688 bimanual mobile manipulator [32] to the SO-101, at about a fortieth of the
price of an ALOHA arm [4]. LeRobot [5] and community data have made the SO-100/101 a training platform
for open VLAs [6, 7]. Four 2026 benchmarks evaluate VLAs on physical SO-101 arms. Yu and Qiu [8] analyse
failure and recovery on four tasks, VLA-REPLICA is a sub-$1,100 kit reproduced across sites [9], ArmnetBench
scores 2,518 rollouts of seven policies on an arm farm [3], and Spa-Bench probes recombinations of familiar
objects, spatial concepts and actions in its primary evaluation, with a separate novel-object pilot [10]. All four
use real robot demonstrations for task-specific adaptation and evaluate on physical hardware. In simulation, the
SO-101 Task Set contains eight language-free tasks for visual reinforcement learning with sim2real transfer [15],
and LeIsaac provides SO-101 teleoperation and data-collection tooling in Isaac Lab [33]. To our knowledge,
SO-101 Bench is the first language-conditioned SO-101 benchmark with held-out object splits whose simulated
policy ranking is validated on the real arm. It also represents one of, if not the most, challenging task suites
handled by an SO-101 up to this point.

Real2sim evaluation and sim2real transfer.  Whether simulated evaluation predicts real performance was
studied early for navigation [34]; for manipulation, SIMPLER [18] showed that an aligned simulator can rank


                                            3real-world policies and introduced the MMRV metric. Twins built from scans, neural reconstructions or generated
assets now report strong score or ranking agreement within their validated settings [19, 20, 35, 36, 37, 38];
SimFoundry reaches Pearson 0.911 and MMRV 0.018 over five policy architectures [21]. Two 2026 results
temper this. Validity does not carry across setups: re-tested against new real rollouts, SIMPLER’s agreement with
the real-robot ranking is weak [22]. Reconstruction quality also matters: an authored object-and-scene pipeline
achieved sim–real correlation of 0.90 versus 0.51 for a default reconstruction in a ten-cell study [39], consistent
with our tuning of each reconstructed object against its physical counterpart (Appendix E). Learned world models
are an alternative evaluator [40], but released models often predict success on verified failures [41]. In parallel,
policies trained only on simulated data now transfer to real robots: MolmoB0T reaches 79.2% on real pick-and-
place without real demonstrations [23], OASIS pairs image-to-3D assets with teleoperation inside simulation [24],
and LEGS and Splat2Act fine-tune pretrained VLAs using only synthetic robot demonstrations [42, 43]. We
deploy five sim-trained policies, including an LLM agent, with identical weights and test whether their ranking
survives.

LLM agents for manipulation.  Language models have long planned over learned skills [44] or written
programs that compose perception and control [45, 46], and hierarchical systems pair high-level language
reasoning with low-level action generation [47, 48]. In 2026 such agents became competitive with end-to-
end policies: coding agents are now benchmarked on manipulation directly [49, 50, 51]; GPT-6 Astra with
direct end-effector tool calls ranked above all forty public-policy entries in its September 2026 RoboDojo
comparison [52, 53]; RoboICL reports higher aggregate progress than its strongest lis

From text 'ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6'.

Federica Ferraguti, Andrea Pertosa, Cristian Secchi, Cesare Fantuzzi, and Marcello Bonfe. A methodology for comparative analysis of collaborative robots for industry 4.0. 2019 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference & Exhibition (DATE), pages 1070-1075, Mar 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.23919/date.2019.8714830, doi:10.23919/date.2019.8714830. This article has 36 citations.

The excerpt provides a comparison table for the KUKA LWR 4+, UR5, and Franka Emika Panda—not the UR5e, ABB YuMi (IRB 14000), or Kinova Gen3. For the UR5, the table lists a payload of 5 kg, repeatability of ±0.1 mm, and end-effector speed of 1000 mm/s. For the Panda, it lists a payload of 3 kg, repeatability of ±0.1 mm, and end-effector speed of 2000 mm/s. No accuracy or price values are reported in this excerpt. The table distinguishes “Technical data” from task-programming and force-related results. ## 1. cowling2026from12to pages 1-3 (Context ID: pqac-00000038)

       From 12 to 200 Demonstrations: How ACT, Diffusion Policy,
           SmolVLA and π0.5 Scale on a Low-Cost Arm


                                      Simon Cowling
                                                      fysical.ai, Denmark
                              simon@fysical.ai



                                                       Abstract

             We trained four widely used imitation-learning policies, ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and
                     π0.5, on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 teleoperated demonstrations of one pick-and-place2026
                  task with distractor objects, using one fixed training recipe per policy. Every trained model was then
                run on a physical SO-101 arm on a fixed set of object placements: 1,340 scored episodes in 126
Oct             blocks.
                 ACT, trained from scratch, rose from 1 success in 40 episodes at 12 demonstrations to 37 in 40 at
                100. π0.5 with its action expert fine-tuned was the best policy when data was scarce (16 of 40 at 1227
                  demonstrations, 28 of 40 at 25) and then stayed near 70%; from 100 demonstrations ACT was ahead,
               by a margin this study does not fully resolve. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50%, and
                 both were affected by a failure to start: SmolVLA’s arm never started moving in 47% of episodes, and
                 Diffusion Policy hardly ever started until an idle lead-in was trimmed from the demonstrations. For
                    π0.5 the fine-tuning recipe mattered more than the amount of data: low-rank adaptation succeeded in 4
                  of 110 episodes, against 130 of 200 for action-expert fine-tuning.[cs.RO]
                From the joint and camera recordings we place every episode on a four-stage ladder (started,
                 reached the ball, carried it, delivered it) and show that for ACT more data moves failures from reaching,
                   to grasping, to none, while the failures π0.5 retains are in grasping. We also measure how weak a
                  ten-episode block is as a measurement (the same checkpoint tested twice differs by 2 successes in 10
               on average), separate seed-to-seed variation from that noise, and audit the human scoring against the
                  recordings. Training length was fixed within each recipe, so the amount of data and the number of
                 times it was seen change together; we state which conclusions survive that confound and which do
                   not.


      1  Introduction


         Low-cost arms and open-source software have made real-robot imitation learning accessible to small
           laboratories and individuals. A SO-101 arm costs a few hundred dollars in parts (Knight et al., 2024), andarXiv:2610.37170v1
           the LeRobot library (Cadene et al., 2024, 2026) provides recording, training and evaluation for a range of
           policies behind one interface. Someone starting a new task therefore faces two practical questions at once:
         which policy to train, and how many demonstrations to record.

           The literature does not answer either question well for this setting. Each policy was introduced
        on different robots, tasks and data volumes. ACT was shown with 50 demonstrations per task on a
         bimanual rig (Zhao et al., 2023), Diffusion Policy on a different set of simulated and real tasks (Chi
            et al., 2023), and the vision-language-action models SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) and π0.5 (Black et al.,
         2025a) after pretraining on large multi-robot datasets. Pretrained models are expected to need fewer task
          demonstrations; models trained from scratch are cheaper to train and run. Recent benchmarks on low-cost
         arms compare several of these policies at one data size, or at a few sizes with twenty trials per model
          (Section 2), which is too few to say which differences are real.

             This paper reports a controlled study of that question on one physical task. We recorded 225
          teleoperated demonstrations of a pick-and-place task with two distractor objects, fixed nested subsets of


                                                  112, 25, 50, 100 and 200 demonstrations, and trained ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and π0.5 on each
subset with several training seeds. Every trained model was run on the arm on ten fixed object placements
under a 30-second limit. In total we scored 1,340 episodes in 126 blocks over 17 days, and recorded joint
states, commanded actions and both camera streams for every episode.

   The contributions are:


    1. Scaling curves for four policies on one physical task. Success against number of demonstrations
     from 12 to 200, with confidence intervals and a trend estimate for each policy, including a reversal
      of order between ACT trained from scratch and fine-tuned π0.5 (Section 4.1).

    2. A stage-by-stage account of failure taken from the recordings. Each episode is placed on a
      four-stage ladder using joint and wrist-camera data, which shows where each policy loses episodes
     and how that shifts with data (Section 4.2).

    3. Initiation failure. Two of the four policies often never start moving. For Diffusion Policy we show
     by intervention on the training data that removing an idle lead-in from the start of the demonstrations
     removes the failure (Section 4.3).

    4. Recipe sensitivity of π0.5. Two fine-tuning recipes that differ in which weights are trained give 4%
     and 65% success across the same data budgets, a larger effect than the amount of data had for any
      policy except ACT (Section 4.4).

    5. How much a block of ten episodes can tell you. Re-tests of the same checkpoint, a separation of
      seed-to-seed variation from measurement noise, and an audit of the operator’s scoring against the
      recordings (Sections 3.6 and 4.5).


1.1  Scope of claims

The study has a narrow base and one structural confound, and both shape how the results should be read.
We state them here; Section 7 gives the full list of limitations.


     • One task, one arm, one operator. The rankings are for this task and setup. We make no claim that
      they transfer to other tasks.

     • Recipes, not architectures. Each policy was trained with one fixed recipe, close to the library’s
     documented defaults. The comparison is between policies as a practitioner would typically run
      them, not between architectures at their best.

     • Fixed training length. The number of training steps was the same at every data budget, so a model
      trained on 200 demonstrations saw each frame about 17 times less often than one trained on 12.
     Where a curve flattens or falls at 100 and 200 demonstrations, this study cannot tell a ceiling from
      under-training (Section 5).

     • Testing was dimmer than training. Main-comparison blocks ran at roughly half the illuminance
      of the demonstrations. All policies faced this shift, though not to an identical degree.


2  Related work


The four policies. ACT (Zhao et al., 2023) is a transformer trained from scratch as a conditional
variational autoencoder that predicts a chunk of future actions.  Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023)
generates an action sequence by iterative denoising. SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) is a compact vision-
language-action model that pairs the SmolVLM backbone (Marafioti et al., 2025) with a flow-matching


                                         2action expert and is pretrained on community-collected LeRobot datasets. π0 (Black et al., 2025b) and
π0.5 (Black et al., 2025a) pair a PaliGemma backbone (Beyer et al., 2024) with a flow-matching action
expert and are pretrained on a much larger multi-robot corpus. All four predict action chunks, and all four
are available in LeRobot, which is what makes a like-for-like comparison practical.


Fine-tuning large policies. A pretrained vision-language-action model can be adapted by training all
weights, by training low-rank adapters (LoRA; Hu et al., 2022), or by training the action expert while
the vision-language backbone is frozen or shielded from its gradients (Driess et al., 2025). The openpi
reference code publishes full fine-tuning configurations for π0.5 and low-memory LoRA configurations
for π0 only (Physical Intelligence, 2025). We are not aware of a published real-robot comparison of these
options for π0.5 across data budgets.


How success scales with demonstrations.  Mandlekar et al. (2021) varied dataset size among other
factors for several offline learning algorithms, mostly in simulation. Lin et al. (2025) found that generali-
sation follows an approximate power law in the number of training environments and objects, and that
diversity matters more than the number of demonstrations in each. Brohan et al. (2023) reported the effect

deploy five sim-trained policies, including an LLM agent, with identical weights and test whether their ranking

LLM agents for manipulation.  Language models have long planned over learned skills [44] or written
programs that compose perception and control [45, 46], and hierarchical systems pair high-level language
reasoning with low-level action generation [47, 48]. In 2026 such agents became competitive with end-to-
end policies: coding agents are now benchmarked on manipulation directly [49, 50, 51]; GPT-6 Astra with
direct end-effector tool calls ranked above all forty public-policy entries in its September 2026 RoboDojo
comparison [52, 53]; RoboICL reports higher aggregate progress than its strongest listed baseline on a thirty-task
subset [54], and PyRUA-Lean exceeds the best public entries in its reported leaderboard snapshot [30]. A parallel
line treats the VLA as a tool: Harness VLA exposes a frozen VLA as a retryable contact-rich primitive [55],
VoLo steers one as an interruptible tool [56], Gemini Robotics ER 2 hands motor execution to any VLA [57],
and a systematic study of such hierarchies finds that model choice and interface jointly shape performance [58].
Harness effects are large. With the same planner and primitives, one study reports that writing code instead
of calling tools raises success from 63.1% to 71.7% [30]; a better harness lets a weaker model beat a stronger
one [59]; and outside robotics the scaffold alone moves accuracy by up to 28 points within one model [60].
These studies usually compare agents with published entries trained under each entry’s own protocol. Simulated
agent evaluations, ours included, commonly pause the simulator while the model computes, which hides its
real-time cost [61], and frontier models controlling physical arms directly are not yet precise or efficient enough
to finish tasks within a practical action budget [62]. SO-101 Bench compares agents and learned policies on the
same episodes after training every learned policy on the same data and compute, ablates harness and model
separately, and runs the agent on the real robot.

Manipulation benchmarks and evaluation practice.  Simulated benchmarks for generalist policies [12, 13,
14, 53, 63] face saturation and train–test overlap. LIBERO instruction conditioning largely selects among
memorized tasks [16]; policies above 90% there fall below 30%, or to zero, under modest perturbations [64, 65];
and an audit of five suites finds shortcut solvability, state-of-the-art gains not established as statistically significant,
creeping overfitting and dependence on the training-data source [25]. Responses include generalization suites [66,
63], capability suites for memory of occluded objects [67] and spatial grounding [10]. Real-world evaluation
has moved to distributed pairwise comparison [68], autonomous evaluation cells [69], and statistical methods
that separate policies with few trials [11, 70]. SO-101 Bench adopts several of these lessons: it separates unseen
instances from unseen classes and keeps part of the latter private, fine-tunes every policy on the same seen-object
data under one compute budget, selects checkpoints on a separate validation set, and reports confidence intervals
over 916 episodes. It also scores two spatial skills that, to our knowledge, few benchmarks test in closed loop:
placing an object between two referents, and rotating a grasped object to fit (PLAN).

3  SO-101 Bench

SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned tabletop manipulation with a single SO-101 arm [1].  It is
designed to test whether a policy can turn semantic understanding into precise physical execution: identifying
the right object among distractors, grasping objects of unfamiliar geometry, and placing them under (often
precise) spatial constraints. Every component below is shared by all evaluated policies.


3.1 Tasks

The benchmark comprises four language-conditioned tasks (Fig. 2), scored as five task families.

       • Place each object in the plastic bin. The pure grasping task: the policy must identify, grasp, transport
       and deposit every object on the table. The bin moves between episodes. We evaluate a 1-object and a
        4-object condition as separate families.

       • Place [object 1] next to [object 2]. The policy must place the target close to a referent without
        disturbing other objects, adding semantic grounding and basic spatial placement.

       • Place [object 1] between [object 2] and [object 3]. The target must end centred between two referents,
       which makes the task sensitive to object extent, orientation and fine placement; it is the most demanding
         task.

       • Move [object 1] [direction]. The policy must push or carry the target along a straight path in a
      commanded direction until it reaches the boundary formed by the next object in its way.

The bin task stresses grounding, grasp strategy and grasp precision; the three spatial tasks additionally require
relational grounding, spatial reasoning, fine-grained placement and robustness to partial occlusion. To keep
language grounding nontrivial, distractors of the same class or colour are included so that class identity alone is
insufficient, and colour words are omitted from instructions unless necessary (i.e when two objects of the same
class are on the table).

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of repeatable benchmark protocols found in the literature that can be used to evaluate robot arm performance. Include columns: Protocol Name, Source (author/year), Venue, What Is Measured, Number of Trials, Success Criterion / Metric, Measuring Tool / Method, Arms Tested, and DOI. Include these protocols:

1. ISO 9283:1998 Position Repeatability Protocol - as applied by Chen 2015, Pollak 2023, Chajon 2026: measures pose repeatability at 5 points in workspace test cube, 30 reps per point at 10/50/100% speed, metric is mean deviation + 3σ, tools include laser tracker, dial indicator, or photogrammetry

2. REPLAB Grasping Benchmark - Yang 2019 ICRA: measures cumulative success rate on 20-object test set, multiple objects placed randomly, grasp = object held 2 sec after lifting, automated sweeping after 10 failed attempts, WidowX arm

3. Tactile Robot Performance Benchmarking - Kirschner 2021 IROS: measures force sensing accuracy and repeatability, 30 repetitions with reference weights, 8N reference force with 0.8kg mass, Pilz PRMS for collision, UR5e and Franka Panda

4. Photogrammetric Position Characterization - Chajon 2026 Robotics: measures planar XY accuracy and repeatability using camera + ArUco markers, 30 reps at 5 target poses, sub-mm results, UR3 tested

5. SO-101 Bench - Hickok 2026 preprint: measures language-conditioned manipulation success, 916 feasibility-checked episodes, 4 tasks across 3 generalization splits, Isaac Lab digital twin, SO-101 arm

6. Blue Repeatability Test - Gealy 2019 ICRA: measures return-to-home repeatability, 133 motions from random dwell locations, OptiTrack motion capture at 100Hz, Blue arm
"}

The evidence that does exist is summarized below, with clear separation of measured values from manufacturer-specified values.

## 2. Independently Measured Data for Low-Cost Arms

### 2.1 WidowX / REPLAB (~$2,000–$3,000)
Yang et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) built the REPLAB benchmark around a WidowX arm. End-effector positioning performance was reported as "positions within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace floor" and "within 1 cm near the center," combining camera-calibration noise with residual control noise (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000012). No separate ISO 9283-style repeatability value was reported. A complete REPLAB cell cost "about 2000 USD" and "under $3,000" including one spare servo per joint (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014). **Endurance data:** "no major breakages in more than 100,000 grasp attempts" and no servo replacements were needed (pqac-00000009). **No backlash, speed, or payload measurements were published.**

### 2.2 Blue — Berkeley Open Arms (~$3,300–$5,000)
Gealy et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236) characterized the Blue 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm. Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (pqac-00000005). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (pqac-00000004). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (pqac-00000006). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (pqac-00000000). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (pqac-00000029). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (pqac-00000030). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (pqac-00000030). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)

Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (pqac-00000038). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031). (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (pqac-00000024), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (pqac-00000016). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (pqac-00000018). ### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (pqac-00000016), substantially better than the UR5e. ### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (pqac-00000039). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (pqac-00000039).

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. **No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). <artifact id="artifact-00"/>

Six protocols from the literature were identified that can be reproduced with your hardware.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (pqac-00000024), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (pqac-00000010) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup."}

# Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms: Independently Measured Performance Data

## 1. Overview

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference papers, and preprints from 2015–2026 was conducted to identify independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, and failure data for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX) and industrial/research arms (UR5e, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova Gen3). The central finding is that **independently measured mechanical characterization data for most low-cost arms is sparse or absent in the published literature**, whereas industrial arms have manufacturer datasheet values that are widely cited but rarely independently verified through pose-repeatability testing. The evidence that does exist is summarized below, with clear separation of measured values from manufacturer-specified values.

## 2. Independently Measured Data for Low-Cost Arms

### 2.1 WidowX / REPLAB (~$2,000–$3,000)
Yang et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) built the REPLAB benchmark around a WidowX arm. End-effector positioning performance was reported as "positions within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace floor" and "within 1 cm near the center," combining camera-calibration noise with residual control noise (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). No separate ISO 9283-style repeatability value was reported. A complete REPLAB cell cost "about 2000 USD" and "under $3,000" including one spare servo per joint (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). **Endurance data:** "no major breakages in more than 100,000 grasp attempts" and no servo replacements were needed (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). **No backlash, speed, or payload measurements were published.**

### 2.2 Blue — Berkeley Open Arms (~$3,300–$5,000)
Gealy et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236) characterized the Blue 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm. Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 5-6). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 1-2). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 6-8). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)
**No published, independently measured repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, speed, or endurance data were found for any of these three arms.** The SO-101 is extensively used in manipulation benchmarks — Hickok (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420) reports 916 feasibility-checked benchmark episodes across four tasks (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4), and Cowling (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170) reports 1,340 scored episodes (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3) — but these measure task-level policy success, not ISO-style mechanical properties. Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6). The UR5e datasheet specifies ±0.03 mm repeatability. The Chajon et al. (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). The benchmarking protocol used 30 repetitions, an 8 N reference force from a 0.8 kg mass, two reference poses, and at least 3 seconds of acquisition per trial (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement for the UR5e was found in the searched literature.**

### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4), substantially better than the UR5e. Ferraguti et al. independently found external force estimation error below "1.5 N RMS" for the Panda, compared with 13 N for the UR5 (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement was found.**

### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8).

## 4. Endurance and Failure Data

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. The robot "showed no significant wear or damage" (guist2023arobustopensource pages 7-8, guist2023arobustopensource pages 2-3). Material cost: approximately €14,185 (guist2023arobustopensource pages 5-6).

**WidowX/REPLAB:** Over 100,000 grasp attempts with zero servo replacements (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3).

**For AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, and ABB YuMi: no published endurance or systematic failure-rate data were found** in the peer-reviewed or preprint literature searched.

## 5. Backlash

**No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). The Forte paper mentions backlash as a design concern but provides no measured value (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). The CloudGripper paper attributes Z-axis variability partly to servo-motor inconsistency but does not quantify backlash separately (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). An open-source test stand for backlash measurement in UART servos (Kotov 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ohx.2026.e00767) was identified but could not be retrieved in full text.

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Where no published evidence exists:**

- **AgileX PiPER:** No published ISO 9283-style repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload capacity, maximum speed, or endurance test. The arm appears in dozens of VLA and embodied AI papers but exclusively at the task-success level.
- **SO-100/SO-101:** No published mechanical characterization despite extensive use in LeRobot and VLA benchmarks. Task-level success is well documented (916+ episodes in SO-101 Bench, 1,340 episodes in Cowling 2026).
- **Koch v1.1:** No published mechanical characterization of any kind.
- **Backlash:** No arm in either the low-cost or industrial category has a published, independently measured backlash value in the retrieved literature.
- **Systematic endurance/failure rates:** No mean-time-between-failure or systematic reliability study was found for any of the arms of interest.

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 3-4) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup.

Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (pqac-00000005). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (pqac-00000004). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (pqac-00000006). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (pqac-00000000). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (pqac-00000029). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (pqac-00000030). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (pqac-00000030). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)
**No published, independently measured repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, speed, or endurance data were found for any of these three arms.** The SO-101 is extensively used in manipulation benchmarks — Hickok (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420) reports 916 feasibility-checked benchmark episodes across four tasks (pqac-00000023), and Cowling (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170) reports 1,340 scored episodes (pqac-00000038) — but these measure task-level policy success, not ISO-style mechanical properties. Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (pqac-00000038). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031). The UR5e datasheet specifies ±0.03 mm repeatability. The Chajon et al. (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (pqac-00000024), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (pqac-00000016). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (pqac-00000018). The benchmarking protocol used 30 repetitions, an 8 N reference force from a 0.8 kg mass, two reference poses, and at least 3 seconds of acquisition per trial (pqac-00000019). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement for the UR5e was found in the searched literature.**

### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (pqac-00000016), substantially better than the UR5e. Ferraguti et al. independently found external force estimation error below "1.5 N RMS" for the Panda, compared with 13 N for the UR5 (pqac-00000018). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement was found.**

### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (pqac-00000039). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (pqac-00000039).

## 4. Endurance and Failure Data

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. The robot "showed no significant wear or damage" (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). Material cost: approximately €14,185 (pqac-00000027).

**WidowX/REPLAB:** Over 100,000 grasp attempts with zero servo replacements (pqac-00000009).

**For AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, and ABB YuMi: no published endurance or systematic failure-rate data were found** in the peer-reviewed or preprint literature searched.

## 5. Backlash

**No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). The Forte paper mentions backlash as a design concern but provides no measured value (pqac-00000002). The CloudGripper paper attributes Z-axis variability partly to servo-motor inconsistency but does not quantify backlash separately (pqac-00000029). An open-source test stand for backlash measurement in UART servos (Kotov 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ohx.2026.e00767) was identified but could not be retrieved in full text.

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Where no published evidence exists:**

- **AgileX PiPER:** No published ISO 9283-style repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload capacity, maximum speed, or endurance test. The arm appears in dozens of VLA and embodied AI papers but exclusively at the task-success level.
- **SO-100/SO-101:** No published mechanical characterization despite extensive use in LeRobot and VLA benchmarks. Task-level success is well documented (916+ episodes in SO-101 Bench, 1,340 episodes in Cowling 2026).
- **Koch v1.1:** No published mechanical characterization of any kind.
- **Backlash:** No arm in either the low-cost or industrial category has a published, independently measured backlash value in the retrieved literature.
- **Systematic endurance/failure rates:** No mean-time-between-failure or systematic reliability study was found for any of the arms of interest.

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (pqac-00000024), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (pqac-00000010) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general ISO 9283 repeatability methodology, but it does not report independently measured repeatability or accuracy values for the UR5e, UR5, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova robot arms, and it gives no prices for those robots or their measurement tools. Under the described protocol, testing uses a workspace test cube and a diagonal test plane containing five poses, P1 through P5. The robot is commanded to visit these poses while its actual end-effector pose is measured. Tests use a consistent unidirectional visitation order, 30 cycles per trial, manufacturer-rated velocities of 10%, 50%, and 100%, and rated payload (optionally also 10% payload). Position repeatability is computed from the measured-point cluster: the barycentre is calculated, distances from each measurement to that barycentre are determined, and the specification is the mean distance plus three standard deviations. Orientation repeatability is separately calculated for three rotation angles using three times the standard deviation. The excerpt mentions recording the actual pose and transforming measurements for axial and radial offsets, but it does not identify a specific measurement instrument or provide arm-specific accuracy results.

It does describe the ISO 9283 path-accuracy methodology used for a FANUC CRX-10iA collaborative robot. Measurements were conducted at 20 °C, using a mechanical flange interface connected to a measuring device, with a maximum load of 10 kg. The robot’s path was measured on a prescribed measuring plane, using bidirectional testing cycles in a workspace section represented by a measuring cube. The experimental setup used the GEPARD measuring system, consisting of a transmitter and receiver. ISO 9283 path accuracy is defined through the maximum deviation between the programmed path and the barycentric line of repeated achieved paths, together with deviations in angular orientation. Positioning accuracy was calculated from measured coordinates at multiple points along the path. The excerpt also notes that measurements may be performed as a function of distance or time, with time-based repetition required when speed fluctuates significantly. It does provide general information about ISO 9283 testing and measurement approaches. ISO 9283 is identified as the international standard for industrial-robot performance criteria and test methods. In the described CRS A255 study, position was measured using a three-dimensional system of dial gauges equipped with capacitive Sylvac systems, with stated measurement accuracy of 0.005 mm. Orientation was excluded because the measurement system only supported linear measurements. Testing followed ISO 9283’s 30-cycle procedure; the experiment was repeated 30 times, producing 900 measurements per target location. Repeatability was assessed using average 3D positional deviation and the standard deviation of that average deviation. Statistical analyses included Friedman’s test for differences among target locations and t-tests for comparing identical locations at different heights. These details may help identify suitable protocols and instruments, but they cannot establish the requested robot-specific performance values or prices.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports positional repeatability measurements for an industrial robot, but it does not identify the robot as Blue (the Berkeley Open Arms platform). In Phase 1, repeatability was measured under unloaded, contact-based conditions. Three contact coordinates were reconstructed geometrically in MATLAB to estimate the end-effector’s sphere center, and 30 consecutive trials were compared with the overall mean center. The resulting repeatability was 0.0260 mm, based on a mean deviation of 0.0096 mm and standard deviation of 0.0055 mm. In Phase 2a, a calibrated external multi-camera vision system recorded the robot’s 3D position over 30 movements between P1 and P2 with a 4 kg test payload; repeatability at P2 was 0.0406 mm. In Phase 2b, the same vision-based system measured five ISO 9283 cube positions under the 4 kg payload. Repeatability values were 0.05810, 0.04974, 0.05159, 0.02691, and 0.26279 mm for P1–P5 respectively, with P5 as an outlier. The excerpt does not provide Blue’s actual payload capacity, price, or position-control bandwidth; the stated 4 kg is only the payload used during these tests.
